finding.claim: Unauthenticated cross-tenant user enumeration: GET /users returns id and name for any org supplied in the query string, with no auth or ownership check.
finding.sink: req.pg.query SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE org = $1 (db.js:9) and res.json(rows) (db.js:10)

trace.note: app.listen(3002) with no host binds all interfaces: public ingress
/users route registered with no auth middleware
org taken from req.query and bound as parameter $1
all matching rows returned, no pagination or rate limit

finding.guards_checked: Parameterized query blocks SQLi but not authz. No app- or route-level auth middleware in file. No check binds org to caller. req.pg defined outside this file; code passes org through unchecked. Severity drops if an upstream gateway enforces auth (not in repo).

verdict.guard_found: none. db.js:8 registers /users with no auth middleware, and there is no app.use() anywhere in the file. db.js:9 binds req.query.org as parameter $1 (parameterized, so SQLi is blocked but authz is not). db.js:10 returns all matching rows with no ownership check. db.js:23 listens with no host argument. req.pg is set outside this repo, so an auth check there is unverifiable from this code.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches db.js (8, 9, 10, 23), and an anonymous request to /users?org=<any> reaches the unfiltered SELECT and res.json at db.js:9-10 with no control in the repo blocking it. The one residual uncertainty is whether an upstream gateway or the req.pg wrapper enforces auth, which is not in this repo; that would lower severity but does not refute the in-file finding.

finding.claim: Possible service-wide DoS: a single unauthenticated request can cause an unhandled promise rejection in the async /users handler, which may crash the process on Node 15+ or under Express 4.
finding.sink: await req.pg.query(...) (db.js:9) rejects; the async handler at db.js:8 has no try/catch

trace.note: async route handler with no try/catch
await req.pg.query rejects if driver/Postgres rejects the NUL-byte parameter
handler exits without a response; rejection is unhandled

finding.guards_checked: Parameterized query does not sanitize NUL bytes. No try/catch and no process unhandledRejection handler in file. Express/Node versions unknown (no package.json). Unverified whether PostgreSQL rejects 0x00 in text params. Drops to MEDIUM or closed if versions or driver differ.

verdict.guard_found: none in db.js: no try/catch around the await at db.js:9 and no process-level unhandledRejection handler. No other source files are present (only db.js and .claude/skills/security-research/*/SKILL.md), so a global handler elsewhere cannot be ruled out.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: the async handler at db.js:8 awaits req.pg.query at db.js:9 with the attacker-controlled req.query.org and no try/catch, so a rejection goes unhandled. Whether this crashes the process depends on details not in the directory. Express 4 does not forward async rejections to the error handler, but Express 5 does (and is the default for a fresh install today), and no package.json or lockfile pins the versions. Node 15+ would then crash on the unhandled rejection. The claim that a NUL byte in a text parameter makes Postgres reject the query is plausible but was not verified against the driver or server. The finding is therefore not confirmable from this code, and it drops to low severity or closed under Express 5.

finding.claim: Malformed name on /file (missing or array-valued) throws a TypeError, and Express's default error handler returns a stack trace outside production.
finding.sink: path.resolve(ROOT, req.query.name) (db.js:14) throws; default error handler renders stack

trace.note: path.resolve called with non-string argument, throws synchronously
not reached; error propagates to Express default handler

finding.guards_checked: No typeof check on req.query.name. Trace reveals internal file paths only. LOW per triage Check 8.

verdict.guard_found: none. Nothing between the request and db.js:14 checks the type of req.query.name, and the containment check at db.js:15 runs after path.resolve has already thrown.
verdict.reason: The route at db.js:13 is anonymous, and a missing or array-valued name makes path.resolve at db.js:14 throw a synchronous TypeError before the check at db.js:15 or sendFile at db.js:16 runs, so Express's default handler reports the error. Its stack trace leaks internal paths outside production, which is low-severity information disclosure as the candidate says, and the claim is otherwise accurate.

finding.claim: /count is unauthenticated, discloses the line count of data.csv, and ignores the execFile error so failures return 200 with an empty body.

trace.note: callback ignores e; res.send(out) runs even on error

finding.guards_checked: execFile uses fixed argv, no shell, no user input (command injection cleared). Disclosure is non-actionable. LOW per triage Check 8.

verdict.guard_found: none. db.js:19 registers `app.get("/count")` with no auth middleware, and db.js has no `app.use` anywhere in the file. db.js:20 calls `execFile("wc", ["-l", "data.csv"], (e, out) => res.send(out))`, so the error argument `e` is ignored and `res.send` runs on every path. Command injection is not possible because argv is fixed and no user input reaches the call.
verdict.reason: The anonymous GET /count route at db.js:19-20 has no auth check, leaks the `wc -l` output for data.csv, and always responds via res.send(out) even when execFile fails (db.js:20), so the candidate's claims hold; the impact is low, as the candidate itself rated it.

finding.claim: Express app has no hardening: X-Powered-By is not disabled and no helmet or equivalent security headers are set.
finding.source: Configuration at app creation, no attacker input
finding.sink: HTTP response headers for all routes

trace.note: const app = express(); with no disable or header middleware

finding.guards_checked: No header middleware present in file. Missing control with no demonstrated primary exploit. LOW hardening note.

verdict.guard_found: none. db.js:5 is `const app = express();` with no app.disable("x-powered-by") and no helmet or header middleware anywhere in the directory. The only grep hits for helmet, x-powered-by, disable, or app.use are in .claude/skills/security-research/output-hardening/SKILL.md:115-137, which is documentation, not app code.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: db.js:5 creates the Express app with no header-hardening control, and the attacker is anonymous, since any client can request /users, /file, or /count and receive the default headers. The claim is factually true but is a low-severity hardening note, not an exploitable vulnerability. The repo's own output-hardening skill (SKILL.md:137) says X-Powered-By should not be reported unless a specific disclosed version has an unpatched CVE, so the finding should be downgraded or dropped rather than reported as a vulnerability.
